claim: Showing an object in its usual role slows use of it in a new role. In Glucksberg's candle problem, a box full of tacks took 11.08 min and 16 of 32 failed, versus 3.67 min and 2 of 32 failed with an empty box. With no cue manipulation, only about 25% find the box-as-platform solution.
agent_test: Give the agent tool-substitution items where the usual-use object is pre-framed in the prompt versus listed neutrally. Compare solve rate at equal tokens.
audit_note: Glucksberg 1964 table (11.08 vs 3.67 min, 16/32 vs 2/32) and Fleck & Weisberg 2004 (25% box solution, N=58) verified; evidence line b19 cites DOI BF03196869 which is a different DOI string than the real paper (BF03196876), harmless.

claim: Functional fixedness grows with age: 5-year-olds are not slowed by seeing the usual function, 6 and 7-year-olds are. Table values: 7-year-olds 40% vs 89% solving, mean 115.3 s vs 28.9 s. Cells are N=10, and the paper's text gives different percentages (18% vs 89%; 64% vs 65% at age 5) from its table.
agent_test: Not testable on an LLM as age. Use only as a warning that fixation comes from learned usage knowledge, so a model with more usage knowledge may be more fixed.

claim: Seeing example solutions makes people copy the examples' features into their own designs without reducing the number of ideas (Smith 1993: creatures .11 vs .24, toys .22 vs .35; Marsh 1996 replicated; Fu 2019 feature transfer 23% vs 15%).
agent_test: Show the agent one or three prior solutions before generation versus none; count copied features by code (G8). Equal tokens.
audit_note: Smith (.11/.24, .22/.35), Marsh replication and Fu 23% vs 15% verified; Fu's effect is borderline (chi2=3.6, p=0.05) and Fu did not measure idea count, which rests on Smith and Marsh.

claim: Copying rises with the number of examples shown (0 to 9 examples; omnibus F(4,75)=5.91). The linear-trend statistic is reported inconsistently inside Marsh 1996 (4.75 vs 3.25).
agent_test: Vary the number of in-context prior ideas (0, 1, 3, 9) and plot feature overlap by code.

claim: Telling people to avoid the examples is not a dependable fix. No effect in Smith 1993 (diverge instruction .33 vs .25 standard), Jansson and Smith 1991 and others; it worked in Chrysikou and Weisberg 2005; in George and Wiley 2020 only examples plus an explicit avoid list lifted originality (d=0.58), examples alone did not, and visual examples hurt. Added in gap search: in people, a per-idea 'search for another path' signal from a trained coder gave a borderline gain (expansion ideas 6.75 vs 4.7, d=.49, N=60) and the opposite signal hurt (2.75, d=.79); in LLMs, plain avoid instructions are unreliable (Pink Elephant paper, old models); the human split is attributed to group vs individual testing or psychology vs engineering students but has not been tested directly.
agent_test: Compare at equal tokens: examples only, examples plus 'do not reuse these', and a named list of banned features checked by code. The banned-list variant has the human support.

claim: New ideas inherit the standard properties of the known category: imagined aliens had a sense organ 99%, an appendage 97% and bilateral symmetry 91% (N=71); a classroom replication found 72% legs and 88% eyes. Constrained tool design adapted, not dropped, Earth tools (handles 23% vs 73%, mouthpieces 39% vs 1%).
agent_test: Ask for novel items in a category; count by code how many keep the base properties. Test whether an explicit list of base properties to vary lowers inheritance.
audit_note: Ward 2002 (99/97/91%, N=71; handles 23 vs 73%, mouthpieces 39 vs 1%) and Birdsell 2019 (legs 72%, eyes 88%, n=25 usable) verified; three of four evidence lines are the same Ward paper, and the replication is small (25 creatures).

claim: The starting points for imagined new items are the most easily recalled category members (output dominance vs imagination frequency r=.486 over 150 animals; .674 without 'human'). Typicality and familiarity predict less well.
agent_test: Sample the model's own first-recalled category members and check whether its novel outputs derive from them; then force a draw from a low-dominance member.

claim: Prior knowledge produces fixation: baseball experts do worse on remote-associate items whose obvious baseball answer is wrong (replicated; extra working memory does not help then), and a mechanical-engineering example fixated only students who knew mechanical engineering.
agent_test: For items whose strong domain association is wrong, compare plain, extra-thinking and sampled-attempt arms at equal tokens. Extra thinking is predicted not to help.
audit_note: Ricks et al. 2007 (knowledge x problem type F(1,52)=5.58, WMC no help on misleading items) verified; Purcell & Gero 1996 exists (Design Studies 17:363-383) and the mechanical-engineering result is only confirmed secondhand via Wang et al. 2023 review; Ricks warns baseball demand may have been guessed.

claim: Presenting examples at a higher level of abstraction (function trees, warnings that name the abstract category) reduced copying and kept or raised originality; the effect was lost when a sketch was added. Seen mostly through reviews, plus one opened primary (hen's egg: a restrictive default path carries most answers). Gap search could not open the primary papers (Atilola 2016, Ezzat 2020, Agogue 2014); effect sizes are still missing and one picture-vs-text effect (Cardoso and Badke-Schaub) failed to replicate.
agent_test: Give the agent a function-level description of prior solutions instead of the solution text, at equal tokens; measure overlap by code.

claim: Taking a break gives a small benefit (mean d=0.29 over 117 studies), larger with an undemanding gap task and for divergent tasks, and it does not help against fixation from domain knowledge. This sits in mild tension with SCHEMA 4b (incubation by distraction not to add).
agent_test: Not an LLM operation. The nearest analogue is a fresh-context restart; test restart vs continue at equal tokens (anytime-search subfield).

claim: Whether examples hurt or help across whole studies is unsettled. The Sio 2015 meta-analysis (43 studies) reports narrower variety but more novel and better ideas (abstract only; paper not opened). A review of 25 studies found 14 manipulated variables. Purcell 1993 failed to replicate Jansson and Smith (snippet only). Gap search tried again to open Sio 2015 and could not (publisher block); only a machine summary was seen, so the numbers stay unverified.
agent_test: Always measure both variety and the quality of the final pick at equal tokens; do not treat reduced variety alone as damage.

claim: A short lecture on how the brain makes associations cut the share of designs with copied flawed features from .88 to .53 in 12 student teams (p=.025). A bad-ideas session did not and cost ideas. No control group; one study.
agent_test: Weak, before and after contrast only. Do not base the schema on it.

claim: The generic parts technique (build a parts tree, replace use-implying descriptions with material and shape words) raised solution rates on eight functional-fixedness insight problems from 49% (untrained control, N=14) to 83% (trained, N=14), t(26)=4.23, p<.001, d about 1.6 by my calculation. The '67% more' in the press release is the relative gain (83/49). The numbers come from the inventors' own later paper, the control had no placebo training, and no replication or LLM test was found.
agent_test: Implement as a prompt operator: list parts, redescribe each without the object name, ask what each could do. Test on MacGyver and tool-substitution items against zero-shot CoT at equal tokens; expect the control rate for a plain agent to be well above 49% on easy items.

claim: LLMs fixate within a session about as much as people: new idea categories accumulate at about one third of the possible rate (slope 1.013 LLM vs 1.035 human, p=.51). Across independent runs LLMs are less diverse (28 vs 22 unique categories; 206 vs 88 combinations).
agent_test: Measure category accumulation slope within one agent run versus across runs, with a category scheme fixed in advance.

claim: LLM idea pools are less diverse than human pools: GPT-4 vs crowd on all four diversity metrics (Ma 2024); GPT-4 pool cosine similarity .255 to .432 vs .243 for humans (Meincke 2024); ChatGPT groups converge more than card-deck groups (d=.47, individual level no difference); 70+ models give same-prompt pairwise similarity above 0.8.
agent_test: Treat samples from one model as correlated (consistent with G4). Measure pool diversity by embedding distance and categories, never by the model's own rating.
audit_note: Ma 2024 (crowd more diverse on all topics/metrics), Meincke (.243 vs .255-.432), Anderson (d=.47 group, individual ns) and Hivemind (>0.8) verified; the Meincke human pool is a student group, a high bar.

claim: Different models share one semantic region even under defixation prompts (cross-model pairwise distance about .21 to .34), so mixing models or vendors does not escape the shared mode.
agent_test: Use a second model as a diversity source only inside a measured test; it is not a free fix.
audit_note: IDEAFix Fig 5a distances .206-.341 and its shared-semantic-space statement, plus Hivemind cross-model similarity, verified; 'small' distance has no human or within-model baseline in IDEAFix, and it is a preprint.

claim: Seeding an LLM with a different human first idea did not raise later diversity. Ordinary personas raised between-run diversity (.635 vs .241) but increased fixation within a run (slope .876 vs 1.013); famous-entrepreneur personas changed nothing.
agent_test: Personas give across-sample variety only. Consistent with G4 (no persona voters on single-answer problems); possibly fine for open ideation.

claim: Structured multi-step prompting raises LLM idea diversity: write short titles, revise to bolder distinct ones, then expand (slope 1.013 to 1.363; categories 18.45 to 24.84); a critique-and-edit step gave the biggest gain among eight methods (Ma 2024); Meincke's chain-of-thought prompt beat simple prompts; 25 method-inspired prompts beat control on novelty by about +10% to +41% (IDEAFix). The same chain did nothing for humans. Most of these were not matched on tokens. Gap search: no source compares these procedures on the quality of the single best pick at equal tokens. At equal candidate counts, listing k answers in one call raised human-rated diversity over single calls (jokes 1.83 to 2.93), one prompt with many personas gave the least diverse set, temperature is a weak lever, and same-model critique-and-edit without an outside check lowered accuracy on reasoning tasks (GPT-3.5 CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 38.1).
agent_test: Compare plain n-sample generation vs title-revise-expand vs critique-edit at equal total tokens; score pool diversity by code and final quality by running.
audit_note: Deng (slopes 1.013->1.363, categories 18.45->24.84, human slope 1.035 vs 1.035), Ma critique-critique best, IDEAFix +10% to +41%, Verbalized Sampling jokes 1.83->2.93 and Huang 75.8->38.1 all verified; Deng human CoT also lowered category count slightly (26.29->25.36), so 'did nothing' holds for slope only.

claim: A generic 'be creative' instruction did not change human reliance on Earth fruit (66% vs 62%, ns; 'not bound by Earth fruit' cut it to 48%), and 'think like Steve Jobs' barely moved GPT-4 pool similarity (.368 vs .377 baseline); in contrast IDEAFix found short explicit divergence prompts ('wild', 'unconventional', 'think outside the box') matched or beat long creativity-method prompts on LLM novelty, though homogenization stayed.
agent_test: Do not add 'be creative' text to the schema. If kept, it must win at equal tokens (G7).
audit_note: Ward 62% vs 66% and Meincke Jobs .368 vs .377 hold, but IDEAFix says the opposite of the last clause: short plain 'think outside the box'/'wild'/'unconventional' prompts did as well as or better than long method prompts, so explicit divergence wording does help LLMs.
claim_before_audit: Generic 'be creative' or 'think outside the box' instructions do little: a be-creative instruction did not change human reliance on Earth fruit (66% vs 62%), 'think like Steve Jobs' gave .368 vs .377 similarity, and short plain 'wild' prompts did not match method prompts.

claim: Asking for several answers with stated probabilities (verbalized sampling) gives 1.6 to 2.1 times the diversity of direct prompting on creative writing and recovers 66.8% of the base model's diversity (vs 23.8% direct after DPO), with compute held fixed. Verified in the paper text.
agent_test: One call asking for k answers with probabilities versus k independent calls at equal tokens; code selects (G5).

claim: AI-generated examples fix people too. Using an image generator for ideas raised copying of the example (fixation score +0.32, Bayes factor 124, N=60, three arms of 20) and lowered fluency; an LLM partner helped on simple tasks and hurt on complex ones (N=204 each); assisted gains did not carry to later solo work.
agent_test: Relevant when the agent is a partner: do not show the agent its own first draft as inspiration without a defixation step.
audit_note: Wadinambiarachchi (+0.32, BF 124, N=60, lower fluency), Cheng & Zhang (N=204 per study, simple vs complex) and Kumar (1,100 participants, no solo carry-over) verified; Cheng's 'LLM partner' is a scripted pool of ideas delivered by an assistant, and the CI upper bound is .55 in the paper.

claim: Default LLMs solve far fewer functional-fixedness style problems than people: MacGyver single-attempt success 35% to 42% vs 65.1% for the average human; BrainTeaser ChatGPT 63% (sentence) and 53% (word) vs 92% human. On CreativityBench (no human baseline) LLMs pick a plausible entity far more often than the right part: gold part-level correctness .19 vs entity correctness .51.
agent_test: Use MacGyver, BrainTeaser and a part-level affordance set as the test bed. Plain model vs scaffold at equal tokens.
audit_note: MacGyver (35-42% vs 65.1%) and BrainTeaser (ChatGPT 63/53 vs 92%) verified, but CreativityBench's .19 vs .51 compares gold part-level to entity correctness within LLMs and has no human baseline, so it does not support 'fewer than people'.
claim_before_audit: Default LLMs solve far fewer functional-fixedness style problems than people: MacGyver single-attempt success 35% to 42% vs 65.1% human; BrainTeaser ChatGPT 63% and 53% vs 92%; CreativityBench gold part-level correctness .19 vs entity correctness .51.

claim: Step-wise self-reflection that checks each step against what the objects afford cut infeasible MacGyver solutions by 9.7% (GPT-4), more than a divergent-convergent prompt (4.3%), which raised efficient solutions more (6.5% vs 2.2%). Chain-of-thought brought GPT-4o to human level (85% vs 85.8%) on tool substitution. The reflection is grounded in object affordances, not free self-critique, which SCHEMA 4b rejects. Gap search: MacGyver compared the reflection prompts only against a vanilla prompt, not against chain of thought, so the head-to-head is untested.
agent_test: Test affordance-checklist reflection vs free reflection vs chain-of-thought only at equal tokens on MacGyver.

claim: Few-shot examples did not change mental-set behaviour in LLMs (extra steps unchanged on equivalence problems), and novel in-context examples changed novelty little (OLMo-7B +15.5% on CoPoet, +5.5% on MacGyver; OLMo-2 slightly down). Haq used 6 problems per condition.
agent_test: Vary the in-context examples (typical vs novel) and measure overlap by code at equal tokens.

claim: Denial prompting (after each correct solution, forbid its technique and ask again) forces divergence on code tasks; single-path self-correction and planning did not explore divergent solutions and lost divergent score.
agent_test: Closest to dropping a constraint (O4): ban the last technique, regenerate. Test against plain resampling at equal tokens.

claim: Across four open-weight models (2,880 responses) injecting a short random-term fact raised LLM-judged creativity (88.1 vs 69.6 baseline) and an unrelated-context fact raised flexibility (12.4 vs 9.4); no context type won on all metrics. In the HAICo system paper, an offline GPT-5 ablation using the 24 participants' prompts found associative-thinking prompting gave higher embedding-based idea diversity than non-associative prompting.
agent_test: Test random remote-concept injection vs plain at equal tokens; judge by pre-set category counts or by running, not by the model.
audit_note: In Wong et al. the highest judged creativity (88.1 vs 69.6) came from random-term context while the flexibility gain (12.4 vs 9.4) came from the unrelated-context type; and in HAICo the associative-prompting diversity gain is an offline GPT-5 ablation run on the 24 participants' prompts, not an outcome of the 24-person user study.
claim_before_audit: Injecting a short unrelated random fact raised judged creativity (88.1 vs 69.6) and flexibility across four open-weight models (2,880 responses); associative prompting raised idea diversity in a 24-person system study.

claim: Models pick a plausible object but miss the right part and mechanism; breaking ideas into typed functional fragments and recombining them (NexusAI, N=14) deepened exploration (1.01 vs 0.47) and coverage (.407 vs .079).
agent_test: Part-level decomposition before choosing a tool or approach, compared with whole-object prompting.

claim: Einstellung-style fixation appears in LLMs: in 5,383 paired medical cases, bias-trap rates were 43% to 66% across models (Sonnet-4.5 43%, GPT-5 52%, Gemini-2.5-pro 61%).
agent_test: Use counterfactual pairs (control vs trap) as a fixation test; supports checking against a held-out variant (G3).

claim: Practising wrong answers (red herrings) in memory worsens later fixation on remote-associate items (repetition F(1,132)=5.17, p=.025); context reinstatement did not matter. LLM side (not ideas, tasks with a key): errors left in the chat history raised later errors in a controlled injection test (Sinha 2026), thinking models and a sliding window removed the effect, and models relied on earlier wrong attempts and wrote longer answers (Laban 2025, 39% average drop).
agent_test: Keep failed attempts out of the retry context, or reduce them to a list of banned items (the agent analogue of no-goods).

claim: A delay between seeing examples and designing does not reduce copying: it did not fade in Smith 1993 (Exp 2, N=91) and rose after one day in Marsh 1996 (F(1,73)=4.74). Chat-template tokens themselves also reduce output diversity.
agent_test: Moving on in time does not remove copying if earlier output stays in context. Test removing earlier output from context.
audit_note: Smith Exp 2 (N=91, delay did not significantly diminish conformity; apparent drop was an order effect), Marsh Exp 3 (F(1,73)=4.74, .169 vs .242) and Yun et al. (template tokens cause diversity collapse) verified; Yun clause is unrelated to the delay finding.

claim: Showing an LLM its own earlier answers is not harmful when paired with an explicit request for something different: in NoveltyBench, in-context regeneration (all earlier answers kept, 'give a different answer') was the best of four methods and brought three frontier models roughly to human-writer diversity over 8 generations, while paraphrasing and a 'be unique' system prompt were only marginal.
agent_test: Compare at equal tokens: independent samples, k-in-one-call, and a running list of earlier answers with 'differ from all of these'. Score pool diversity by code.

claim: Errors left in context raise later errors. In controlled injection tests the odds of a mistake rose with the share of earlier wrong turns (Qwen3, Gemma3 and frontier non-thinking models), thinking mode removed the effect, and a sliding context window reduced it. In multi-turn tasks models relied on their first attempts and produced 20 to 300% longer answers. Scope: tasks with one right answer, not idea generation.
agent_test: Restart from the task statement plus a short no-good list instead of appending raw failed drafts. Test restart vs append at equal tokens on a task with a key.
audit_note: Sinha (self-conditioning, thinking fixes it, sliding window improves) and Laban (answer bloat 20-300%) verified; 'odds' is loose wording for turn-accuracy decline and Sinha says larger models were more prone.

claim: Same-model critique-and-edit without an outside check does not reliably help and can hurt: GPT-3.5 CommonSenseQA fell from 75.8 to 38.1 after one self-correction round, GPT-4 GSM8K from 95.5 to 89.0 after two. The reported gains in earlier work used oracle labels. A human analogue of an outside check (per-idea 'search elsewhere' signals) gave only borderline gains.
agent_test: Any critique-and-edit step needs a code, test or held-out check that can say 'no change'. Otherwise count it as a cost.

claim: Reasoning-trained models are not immune to Einstellung-style items. On 100 mARC-QA clinical items DeepSeek-R1 scored 52%, DeepSeek-V3 50%, Gemini-1.5-pro 50% and o1 48% against 66% for physicians, with high confidence on wrong answers; MedEinst showed trap rates of 43% to 66%. The R1 vs V3 gap is two points with no separate test.
agent_test: Use a counterfactual pair with a fixed key as the standing fixation probe; do not assume extra thinking removes the pull.
audit_note: mARC-QA (52/50/50/48 vs 66%, p values) and MedEinst (5,383 pairs, 17 LLMs, trap rates 42.98-60.90 and up to 66.1) verified; 43-66% is the span across the models quoted, not all 17.

claim: A plain 'do not mention X' line is unreliable for chat models: in the Pink Elephant paper OpenHermes baselines mentioned the banned entity as often or more often when told to avoid it, and GPT-4 still mentioned it at a rate near 0.13 against a base rate of 0.33 (table partly garbled). A code check of the output plus regeneration is the dependable form.
agent_test: Compare free 'avoid these' text with a code-checked banned list (string or category match, regenerate on hit) at equal tokens; count extra calls.

claim: Judge noise differs a lot by probe. Human agreement on diversity (Gwet AC1) was 0.86 for jokes, 0.87 for stories and 0.54 for poems; on quality 0.79, 0.64 and 0.49 (story lowest). The category-accumulation slope of Deng rests on one GPT-4o coder with no agreement figure. Probes with a fixed answer key (tool-choice items, counterfactual pairs) have no judge noise.
agent_test: Standing fixation probe: prefer a keyed item (counterfactual pair or tool-substitution multiple choice). If using category slope, fix categories in advance and recode with a second model.

claim: At equal candidate counts, asking for k answers in one call (Sequence) raised human-rated diversity over single calls on jokes (1.83 to 2.93) and a little on poems and stories (1.90 to 2.07; 2.74 to 2.76); verbalized sampling added little over Sequence on jokes (3.01) but more on poems (2.39) and stories (3.06). Putting many personas into one prompt gave the least diverse set; separate calls did better.
agent_test: Test k-in-one-call as the default baseline before adding any defixation operator.

claim: Temperature is a weak lever for diversity or novelty: at 1.5 versus 1.0 GPT-4o categories rose from 22 to 23 against 28 for humans, at 2.0 output was garbled, and story novelty correlated only weakly with temperature while coherence fell.
agent_test: Do not spend tokens on temperature sweeps as a defixation method.
audit_note: Deng Appendix F (22 vs 23 categories, humans 28, garbled at 2.0) and Peeperkorn (weak novelty correlation, moderate coherence loss) verified; the two come from different tasks (ideas vs stories), which the claim joins loosely.

claim: A plateau signal can break LLM fixation on one concept: in a hackathon ChatGPT kept refining a concept after returns shrank and pivoted when told performance had plateaued and to test an original idea. It also fixed on the last item of a list in the prompt. Qualitative, one run.
agent_test: Code-side plateau detector (no gain over n rounds) that forces a return to an earlier branch; shuffle list order in prompts.

claim: MacGyver's reflection prompts were tested only against a vanilla prompt. Whether affordance reflection beats plain chain of thought for current models is untested; GPT-4o with CoT already matched humans (85% vs 85.8%) on a four-option tool-choice version.
agent_test: Run vanilla vs zero-shot CoT vs affordance-reflection at equal tokens on MacGyver; only then add the operator.
